voiceover: Does the Qur'an confirm the very Scriptures it contradicts? The Qur'an calls itself musaddiq — the confirmer of the Scriptures that came before it. It affirms the Torah given to Moses and the Gospel given to Jesus as revelation from the same God — 'confirming what was before it.' It even tells Christians to judge by their own book: 'let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein.' So the Qur'an holds up the Gospel as a true standard from God. But that Gospel — the one in the hands of the Christians of Muhammad's day — teaches what Islam denies. It says Jesus was crucified, and that he is the divine Son of God. The Qur'an denies both. So the Qur'an confirms a book that contradicts it. And the whole case is built from the Qur'an's own words. A Muslim will answer: the Qur'an guards the true Gospel — it needn't ratify every line of today's Bible. That's a fair reply, and it genuinely narrows the argument. But the Qur'an still sent Muhammad to consult the Scripture the people of his own day held in their hands — and the case never needed a perfect Bible, only the one they already had. A shared premise, turned on the system by its own words — not a claim that the two faiths teach the same thing. That's the dilemma. It's the argument at the heart of Christopher Frost's book, The Islamic Dilemma. Read it together, chapter by chapter, in our reading club.
